quarterly_data.signal: Q3 FY2026 CALL (December quarter) - HEADLINE: record third quarter. Revenue grew 26% year on year to $1.24 billion, the fourth consecutive billion-dollar quarter. Royalties rose 27% to a record $737 million on record units, led by smartphones (higher royalty rates per chip) and the data center (triple-digit YoY growth); automotive grew double digits. CFO Jason Child: 'we thought we'd grow about 20%. We grew 27%' (a '$30 million beat or more'). License and other revenue was $505 million, up 25%, with two new Arm Total Access Agreements and two new CSS licenses, both with leading smartphone handset OEMs. Annualized contract value (ACV) grew 28% YoY, the same 28% as in Q2 and Q1 and above the long-term mid-to-high-single-digit expectation for license revenue. Non-GAAP opex was $716 million, up 37% on R&D headcount. Non-GAAP operating income was $505 million (+14%), an operating margin of about 41%. Non-GAAP EPS was $0.43, close to the high end of guidance.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $1.24 billion (+26%); royalty $737 million (+27%); license $505 million (+25%); ACV +28%; non-GAAP EPS $0.43; operating margin about 41%

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 FY2026 GUIDANCE (given on the Q3 call): revenue $1.47 billion plus or minus $50 million, about 18% YoY growth at the midpoint. Royalties are guided up low teens YoY and licensing up high teens YoY. Non-GAAP opex approximately $745 million; non-GAAP EPS $0.58 plus or minus $0.04. Child said the low-teens royalty growth reflects seasonality (calendar Q1 is one of the slower quarters) and lapping an unusually timed MediaTek chip release a year earlier; the memory impact is 'very minimal'. He still expects Q4 royalties to be 'stronger than what we previously expected' and full-year royalties 'in that north of you know, 20% range'. Full year FY2026: 'we said at least 20%, and I think now we're guiding to '22 at the midpoint'. FY2027 has no formal guide, but 'the 20% growth rate I think, certainly is very reasonable'. No FY2028 view yet: 'other possible offerings' are still being worked through. Opex: the Q4-to-Q1 step-up should be similar to last year's low-double-digit sequential growth, then moderate. The SoftBank licensing/design-services contribution is 'the right run rate going forward'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 FY2026 guide $1.47 billion, plus or minus $50 million (about 18%); non-GAAP EPS $0.58, plus or minus $0.04; opex approximately $745 million

quarterly_data.signal: CLOUD AI / DATA CENTER: CEO Rene Haas said data center royalty revenue 'has grown more than 100% year on year' and continues to double YoY. The drivers are the ramp of Arm-based chips at all major hyperscaler companies and 'ongoing share gains from custom hyperscaler chips'. The AI data-center build-out also lifts deployments of networking chips, particularly DPUs and smart NICs, where Arm says it has a very high market share. Arm expects its share among the top hyperscalers to reach 50%. Sizing (disclosed once a year): data center was double-digit % of revenue at the start of the year and should now be 'somewhere in kind of the teens to probably getting closer to 20%'. Over the next two to three years it should match or exceed the smartphone business, which is '40 to 45% of total business'. Haas: 'in a few years our data center business to be our largest business, larger than mobile'. Arm has reorganized into three business units: Edge AI (smartphone, IoT), Physical AI (automotive, robotics) and Cloud AI (data center, networking). In Physical AI, Rivian's third-generation autonomy computer is the first production vehicle on a custom Arm chip, and Tesla's upcoming Optimus humanoid robot is powered by a custom Arm-based AI processor.
quarterly_data.figure: data center royalty more than 100% YoY; data center teens to closer to 20% of revenue vs smartphone 40 to 45%; top-hyperscaler share expected to reach 50%

quarterly_data.signal: AGENTIC INFERENCE RAISES CPU CONTENT: AI is shifting from training to inference, and that inference is increasingly agent-based: 'persistent, always on, and power constrained'. Agent coordination runs on CPUs, so customers want higher core counts and better power efficiency. Haas said the latest hyperscaler and NVIDIA CPU generations 'have increased the number of cores. And we think that only continues.' He cited four examples. AWS's fifth-generation Graviton has 192 cores, double Graviton4. NVIDIA's Vera has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Microsoft's Cobalt 200 has 132 cores on Neoverse CSS V3, up from 128 in Cobalt 100 on Neoverse N2. Google previewed its second Arm server processor (Axion-powered m4a instances). Integrated platforms raise output per watt: AWS pairs Graviton with Arm-based Nitro DPUs and training accelerators, and NVIDIA pairs GPUs with Arm-based CPUs and BlueField. Over the next three years Haas expects CPUs to take on work GPUs used to do and more custom CPU-based chips to appear. He also sees specific prefill/decode inference solutions continuing to extend.
quarterly_data.figure: Graviton 192 cores; Vera 88 cores (vs 72); Cobalt 200 132 cores (vs 128)

quarterly_data.signal: COMPUTE SUBSYSTEMS (CSS): nearly two and a half years after launch, demand 'continues to exceed expectations'. Two more CSS licenses were signed in the quarter (Edge AI tablets and smartphones), for a total of 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies. Five customers now ship CSS-based chips, two of them on a second-generation platform, and the top four Android smartphone vendors ship CSS-powered devices. CSS was 'approaching double digit' of royalties last year and is 'into the teens' this year. Child said it 'could be upwards of 50%' over the next couple of years, and every CSS customer that could renew for the next generation has done so. Each smartphone cycle brings a new CSS, generally at a higher royalty rate. Haas sees no bill-of-materials pushback: fabs moving from five to three to two nanometer shorten design windows, so faster time to market is worth more than the cost. Neoverse CSS V3 underpins Microsoft's Cobalt 200.
quarterly_data.figure: 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies; five customers shipping CSS chips; CSS royalty share into the teens, could be upwards of 50%

quarterly_data.signal: MEMORY SHORTAGE vs SMARTPHONE ROYALTIES: Child noted that MediaTek talked about 'around a 15% reduction in unit volume for next year', in line with other handset makers' views on memory supply constraints. Partners are protecting the premium/flagship tier, where Arm's CSS and v9 royalties sit; the constraints should mostly hit the low end (v8 and older, with much smaller royalties). A 20% volume reduction would hit smartphone royalties by 'somewhere around a 2% or 4% at worst'. In a later answer he put it at 'at most a kind of four to 6%' within smartphones, already including contractually agreed higher per-unit rates. The effect on total royalties would be 'a 1%, maybe 2% negative impact', more than offset by cloud AI growing ahead of expectations. Memory impact on the Q4 guide is 'very minimal', and memory and other shortages affect Arm less than full-fab semiconductor companies. Haas added that Arm is highly involved in research on SRAM and alternative memory technologies for AI.
quarterly_data.figure: 20% smartphone unit cut -> 2% or 4% at worst (at most four to 6%) smartphone royalty impact; 1%, maybe 2% on total royalties

quarterly_data.signal: INVESTMENT / NEXT CATALYST: rising R&D spend funds next-generation architectures, compute subsystems and 'our exploration into chiplets and complete SoCs'. The growing base of 'long-duration contracts at structurally higher royalty rates' gives Arm the confidence to invest in 'next-generation architectures, compute subsystems, and silicon'. Arm will host an event on March 24 but gave no details ahead of it. Asked whether SoftBank could get an Arm custom ASIC, Child said nothing could be shared about specific products.

Google previewed its second Arm-based server processor. Its Axion-powered m4a instances (as transcribed) deliver up to 2x better price performance and 80% better performance per watt than comparable x86 offerings. Google has now migrated over 30,000 applications to the Arm instruction set.

contracts.signal: Of Q3 license revenue of $505 million, Arm's 'agreement with SoftBank for Technology Licensing and Design Services contributed $200 million'. CFO Child: 'SoftBank has become an increasingly important customer as they build out their AI compute strategy, including their recent acquisitions such as Ampere and Graphcore'. Arm believes the SoftBank revenues 'are durable as they relate to current generations'. The prior quarter was '$178 for the quarter'; the step-up to about $200 is 'just a full quarter impact' and no new deals were signed. 'I would expect that $200 going forward is the right run rate going forward.' Asked about a possible Arm custom ASIC for SoftBank, management would not comment on specific products.
